fields.meaning: So-called… | That is, it is precisely…
examples: Is it true that he isn't coming?
I was relieved to hear that she had passed.
I was told the deadline was today, so I hurried to submit it.
This is enough, that's what I'm saying. You don't need to buy any more.
You call this justice? I can't accept that.
Going to Japan has been my dream for a long time.
fields.explain:
というの has an explanatory/emotional tone; ということ is more objective and abstract.
In casual speech, というの → っていうの; in formal written language, ということ is preferred.
With というのか , intonation is important to express a question with a somewhat contradicting tone.
というので is often used when the reason is indirect information (heard/believed that).

• ① Affirmation / emphasis: Used when the speaker wants to strongly affirm what they just stated or draw a conclusion from previous information.
→ “That is…”, “It means…”.
• ② Conveying information (reported speech): Means “I hear that…”. More formal than「～そうだ」「～らしい」.
• ③ Emphasizing emotion, explaining a reason: May carry surprise, reproach, or an assertion of what is right.
• More formal than というんだ / っていうんだ. Used in written language, speeches, essays, and explanatory texts.
fields.notes:
• Often used in written language, reports, news, and speeches.
• In casual conversation, Japanese people often say: ～っていうんだ.
• Can carry a judgmental emotion: “You're saying that…?”, “You mean…?”
mistakes: Confusing ということ with というの: in academic writing, use ということ and avoid というの.
Attaching です/ます before というの: 来ますというの (unnatural) → 来るというの.
Using というのか too strongly in polite language → it can easily sound aggressive.

examples: Our homeroom teacher, Yamada-sensei, is very young and seems more like a friend than a teacher.
The air conditioning in the office was too strong; it was cold rather than cool.
Losing the match was not so much disappointing as simply frustrating.
For me, studying abroad was not so much a way to learn about the outside world as a means of leaving home.

This movie is sad rather than scary.
fields.explain:
Used to rephrase an expression, emphasizing that B is more fitting than A.
Has a mildly contradicting nuance and is polite if used skillfully; add むしろ to emphasize “contrary to expectation”.
Suitable for describing impressions and evaluations; avoid it when a completely neutral statement is needed.
In spoken language, it can be replaced by というか (lighter) or っていうか (very colloquial).

• Literally “it is more correct to say A than B”, but in actual usage it negates/adjusts A and affirms that B is the more fitting expression. Natural translation: “not so much A as B”, “rather than A, it should be called B”.
• A is a general or old description/label; B is the essence/core point the speaker wants to emphasize.
• Often carries a nuance of rephrasing, correcting oneself, or subjective evaluation; stronger in degree than というか (which works as a filler).
• Often used to compare qualities and impressions: “beautiful… rather than cute”, “hot… rather than warm”.
• With むしろ: highlights the reversal of expectation, “it should really be B”.
fields.notes:
• With nouns/na-adjectives, だ before というより is usually omitted; だというより is not wrong but is more formal.
• A can be fairly negative to set off a positive B (or vice versa) for rhetorical effect.
• In polite disagreement, you can begin with: どちらかというと/私の印象では…＋B。
meaning: 「～という言い方より…という言い方の方が適切だ。」 ～より、もっと適切な言い方（…）を示すときに使う
The expression … is more appropriate than the expression ~.
Used when you want to point out that the expression … is more appropriate than the expression ~.
examples: 1. ぼくと彼が友達？ いや、僕たちは友だちというよりいい競争相手なんだよ。
He and I are friends? No, we're more like good rivals than friends.
2. 美知子は歩くのが速い。歩くというより走るという感じだ。
美知子 walks fast. It's more like running than walking.
3. A 「へえ、この絵、社長に頼まれてかいたんですか。」
B 「頼まれて、というより命令されたんだよ。」
mistakes: Reversing the order of A/B: it must be “AというよりB” (B is the main point).
Adding an unnecessary だ: “先生だというより” is not wrong, but “先生というより” is usually more natural.
Using it when A and B are not on the same axis of comparison: they should belong to the same category/quality to be logical.
Confusing it with AよりB (ordinary comparison) in JLPT questions: というより has the nuance of “correcting the expression”.

fields.meaning: Speaking of… (evoking an association: といえば)
examples: Speaking of Japanese food, sushi is the famous one, isn't it?
Speaking of Mother's Day, carnations come to mind right away, but other flowers are fine too, you know.

A: I saw Mt. Fuji from the train window this morning. It was really beautiful.
B: Oh yeah? Speaking of Mt. Fuji, I heard Tanaka is going to climb it next month.
※In casual conversation, it becomes 「っていえば」.
fields.explain:
◎ An expression that picks up a word from the flow of the conversation and talks about something related to it.
◎ Mentions something one has been reminded of by something just said in the conversation.
fields.notes:
meaning: Speaking of ~, mentioning ~, when it comes to ~
examples: 1. 日本料理といえば、おすしや天ぷらが人気だ。
Speaking of Japanese food, sushi and tempura are very popular.
2. 夏といえば、やっぱり海へ行きたくなる。
Speaking of summer, it makes you want to go to the sea.
3. 日本と言えば、何が思い浮かびますか。
When it comes to Japan, what comes to your mind?
4. 心理学と言えば、確か、田中さんが専門だって言っていた。
Speaking of psychology, that reminds me, I think it's Tanaka's major. | Variant: ～といったら

examples: "Kim, I hear you studied Russian in college."
"Yes, but even though I say I studied it, it was only at the beginner level."
"My new apartment is far from the station, you know."
"But even if it's far, it's only a 15-minute walk, right?"
"The area around the station may be lively during the day, but there aren't many people around at night."
There are many detached houses in this area. But even though they're detached houses, the lots are about 90 square meters at most.
fields.explain:
B uses real information to adjust the expectation set up by A; often appears in explanations and when being modest.
Common in natural conversation; can also be used in neutral written language.
Rarely used to lead into a command/suggestion; usually states facts, evaluations, or habits.

• “Although it is called A… (actually) B”: states a label/concept A, then lowers expectations and clarifies the reality B.
• Emphasizes the gap between a name/stereotype and reality: “it's called cheap, but it's actually not that cheap…”.
• Often used to set a limitation on scope, degree, or exceptions; B is usually information that corrects expectations.
• Concessive nuance, more objective than けど/が, with little strong emotion.
fields.notes:
• A is usually a “label/title”: a season, job title, nationality, state…
• When you need to be humble: できるといっても、少しだけです。
• B can express partial negation of the expectation, or give an exception/limiting condition.
mistakes: B has the wrong function (command/suggestion): avoid “Aといっても、〜してください/〜ましょう”.
Confusing it with とはいえ in terms of style: if the question requires a formal nuance → choose とはいえ.
A is not a “label”, so the sentence sounds forced: prefer A as a general frame and B as the specific reality.

examples: As we decided last week, the meeting will be held from 6 o'clock.

fields.explain: ◎ Expresses doing something exactly as promised, planned, or instructed.
fields.notes:
examples: 1. わたしが　やった　とおりに、やって　ください。
Please do it exactly the way I did.
2. 見た　とおりに　話して　ください。
Please tell us exactly what you saw.
3. 線のとおりに　紙を　折りました。
I folded the paper along the line.
explain: Also used for commands/instructions: ～とおりにしてください.
Emphasizes exactness according to a model/standard (a drawing, a procedure, instructions).
Meaning “just as expected/planned”: ～のとおりだ/だった.
In casual use, “Nどおり” is common; in formal/precise use, the full “Nのとおり” is used.
Not used for loose “similar” comparisons without a standard; in that case ように is more natural.
examples: 1. 説明書に書いてあるとおりに組み立ててください。
Please assemble it exactly as written in the instructions.
2. 先生が言ったとおりに発音すれば通じます。
If you pronounce it exactly as the teacher said, you'll be understood.
3. 試合は予想どおりの結果になった。
The match ended with the expected result.
4. 写真のとおり、部屋はとても広いです。
Just as in the photo, the room is very spacious.
5. いつもどおり落ち着いてやれば大丈夫だ。
If you stay calm and do it as usual, you'll be fine.
meaning: Exactly as…/Just like…
Just as (expected/planned/instructed/hoped…)
As you have seen/know…
explain: Expresses an action or result that happens exactly as was said, seen, heard, or demonstrated. Emphasizes “exactly like that”.
Used with nouns such as prediction, plan, instruction, order, expectation… to say that the result turned out as anticipated.
A formal expression, often used in presentations: “as you have seen/know/heard…”. Used a lot in polite spoken language and announcements.
examples: 1. 学生たちは、先生が黒板に書いたとおりにノートに写した。
The students copied into their notebooks exactly what the teacher wrote on the blackboard.
2. 外国語だと、なかなか思ったとおりに話すことができない。
In a foreign language, it's hard to speak exactly the way you want.
3. 父は、私たち家族が父の言うとおりにしないと、きげんが悪い。
My father gets in a bad mood if our family doesn't do as he says.
4. 勉強がなかなか予定どおりに進まない。
My studies aren't progressing as planned.
5. 幼い弟は思いどおりにならないと大声で泣く。
Whenever things don't go his way, my little brother cries loudly.
6. 例のとおりに書きなさい。
Write it exactly like the example.
examples: 1. 交番で教えてもらったとおりに歩いていったので、迷わず会場に着いた。
I walked exactly as I was told at the police box, so I got to the venue without getting lost.
2. 初めて作る料理だから、この本に書いてあるとおりのやり方で作ってみよう。
Since it's my first time making this dish, I'll try making it exactly the way this book says.
3. サッカーの試合の結果はわたしたちの期待どおりだった。
The result of the soccer match was just as we had hoped.
explain: An action that is performed continuously
Used to indicate that an action is performed exactly according to the content expressed by the noun.
examples: 1. 友達がかいてくれた地図のとおりに来たが、道に迷った。
I came following the map my friend drew for me, but I got lost.
2. 雪が降ってきた。予定どおりだ。
It has started snowing. Just as predicted.
3. 先生が言ったとおり、試験は難しかった。
Just as the teacher said, the exam was difficult.
meaning: As, just like
explain: Used to indicate that something proceeds exactly according to the content stated before.
examples: 1. 友達が言ったとおり、日本の物価は高い。
Just as my friend said, prices in Japan are high.
2. 自分の思うとおりに生きることは難しい。
Living exactly as you wish is really hard.
3. 希望どおり
Just as hoped.
4. アドバイスどおり
Following the advice.
mistakes: Confusing “Nどおり” with “Nのどおり”: after a noun to form a compound word, use “どおり”, without inserting “の”.
Using とおり instead of ように when you mean a general “like” → the nuance easily becomes wrong. For example, to describe a style, use ように.
Forgetting “に” with a verb: ×先生が言ったとおり書く → ◯先生が言ったとおりに書く.
Confusing it with “通り” meaning “street”: the 文脈 decides; do not translate mechanically.

fields.connection: [what was expected] + ところが + [contrary result]
examples: I thought I'd make it in time if I left early. However, there was a huge traffic jam because of an accident.
Taking the medicine should have cured it. However, the fever went up.
He promised he would come. However, he never showed up.
I thought the test was easy. However, the average score turned out to be low.
I thought I had contacted them. However, the message hadn't reached them.
fields.explain:
Used when there is a clear “gap between expectation and reality”; creates a sense of surprise and irony.
Can be used in both spoken and written language; somewhat more formal than でも, close to しかし but with a stronger nuance of “surprise”.
Avoid following it with a command/suggestion/volition: use でも/しかし instead if needed.

• A conjunction meaning “however/who would have thought”: presents an actual result completely contrary to an earlier prediction or plan.
• Carries a nuance of surprise and the unexpected; the degree of reversal is stronger than でも/しかし in many contexts.
• The second clause must be a fact that has occurred, not the speaker's volition/suggestion.
fields.notes:
• It often stands at the beginning of a sentence followed by a comma: ところが、… to emphasize the turn.
• Suits narration/storytelling: clause 1 is a “reasonable premise”, clause 2 is “the twist”.
• In emails/when presenting risks, ところが helps make clear that it was an “unavoidable incident”. explain: Often used to negate a conjecture, plan, or thought about a matter or action ⏐ examples: 1. 昨夜はコンサートに行くつもりだった。ところが病気で行けなくなった。
Last night I was planning to go to a concert. However, I got sick and couldn't go.
2. 田中さんは私より若いと思っていた。ところが私より５歳も年上だった。
I thought Tanaka was younger than me. However, Tanaka turned out to be a full 5 years older.
mistakes: Using it with volition/suggestion in the second clause: ×「雨だ。ところが、行きましょう。」→ use でも/しかし.
Confusing it with しかし in sentences without an element of “surprise”: if the question emphasizes surprise → choose ところが.
Using it when the two clauses contrast only slightly: not strong enough → しかし/だが is more natural.

fields.connection: V plain form + とすれば としたら とすると / N + だ / Na + だ / Aい
examples: If I had to choose one of these, I'd go with the one on the far right.
If the world were to end today, I'd probably eat a steak as my last meal.
If he doesn't come, we'll postpone the meeting.
Supposing tomorrow were a day off, where would you want to go?
If this plan were to fail, what would the cause be?
If an earthquake were to happen, what should we do first?
fields.explain:
Suitable for discussions, planning, scientific suppositions, and hypothetical-situation questions.
Rarely used for habits/real conditions. For real conditions, use なら/たら.
Comes before the concluding clause and is often accompanied by conjecture: ～だろう／かもしれない／と思う.
More formal than とすれば; softer than とすると (which has a more logical/technical nuance).

• Supposing/if we assume that ~, then…; used to state a consequence or a choice based on a hypothesis.
• Often used for situations that “may not happen”, leaning toward conjecture, planning, or asking for opinions.
• Often accompanied by どうする／どうなる／だろう／でしょう／場合は…など.
• More formal in nuance than なら; rarely used for conditions that already are/have been true.
fields.notes:
• At the beginning of the sentence, もし is often added to make the suppositional nuance clear: もし～としたら.
• In academic writing, the flow is: 前提Aだとしたら→仮説→検証/示唆…
• Avoid using it when the condition has been confirmed, as it sounds roundabout/distant.
mistakes: Using ～としたら for a certain condition: replace it with なら/たら.
Forgetting だ with N/na: × 学生としたら → 〇 学生だとしたら.
Confusing it with ～としても (concession) in sentences that require the emphasis “even if”: choose ～としても.
～としたら is usually followed by a conjecture/conclusion; avoid abruptly attaching a strong command directly.

examples: I'm an international student now, but I once came to Japan before as a tourist.

fields.explain:
Formal-neutral; usable in both spoken and written language.
Often appears in contexts of profession, social status, legal capacity, or a role within a group.
としては emphasizes a standpoint; としての links the following noun to the role.
Not used directly with adjectives; you must go through nominalization or choose another structure.

• Specifying a role/capacity: states a position, title, or status as the basis for speaking/acting.
• Modifier expressing a quality with としての + N: emphasizes characteristics and responsibilities tied to the role.
• Viewpoint/evaluation with としては: “from the standpoint of…, …”.
• Hypothetical concession with としても: “even as…, still…”.
fields.notes:
• The noun before として should be a noun that clearly indicates a role (教師, 専門家, 親, 市民...). Abstract nouns may need further nominalization.
• When the subject is not shown, the context usually implies “the capacity of the sentence's subject”.
• In job applications/self-promotion: 〜としての強み/経験/実績 are frequently occurring phrases. meaning: As/in the position of/ As/in the position of…, then/ Even as/in the position of… ⏐ explain: Used when talking about a thing or person as a representative of, or an individual belonging to, a general group ⏐ examples: 1. 彼は外国人だが、日本代表として試合に出る。
He is a foreigner, but he plays in the match as a representative of Japan.
2. 彼女は女性としても女優としても最高だが、妻としてはどうだろう。
She is wonderful both as a woman and as an actress, but how is she as a wife?
mistakes: Confusing として with にとって: the former means “role”, the latter “for (from the viewpoint of)”.
Leaving out の in としての + N when it modifies a noun.
Using として directly with an adjective: incorrect; a noun/role concept is needed.
